docs.title: Prepare a bootstrap node
docs.text:
The bootstrap node runs the NKP CLI, Docker, and the temporary kind cluster used to create the management cluster. You can create the VM with the included OpenTofu module or prepare it manually.

The bootstrap node is an execution host, not a special NKP appliance or Kubernetes node. It can be:

  • a Linux VM or physical Linux machine;
  • an administrator's Linux workstation;
  • a macOS workstation or MacBook;
  • the Ubuntu 24.04 VM created by the included OpenTofu module.

Ubuntu is used in these examples because it is straightforward to automate on Nutanix AHV. Other Linux distributions work when the required NKP CLI build, container runtime, and tools are available.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Whichever host you choose needs:

  • Docker with support for Linux containers;
  • kubectl, yq, Git, and jq;
  • an NKP CLI binary matching the host operating system and CPU architecture;
  • network access to Prism Central, Prism Element, cluster networks, required registries, and package sources.

Provide at least 4 CPU cores, 8 GiB memory, and 100 GiB available disk space. Air-gapped bundle handling can require more disk space.

Check CPU architecture

Before using an Apple Silicon Mac or ARM Linux host, confirm that the NKP CLI and bootstrap container images for your NKP release support arm64. Otherwise, use an x86_64 Linux VM. Container emulation can be slower and might not be supported for every release.

docs.title: Option 1: OpenTofu
docs.text:
The included module creates the VM and configures it with cloud-init. It uses standard .tf files because OpenTofu uses the HCL file format.

This option requires OpenTofu 1.8 or later, access to Prism Central, an Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image, a suitable subnet, and an SSH public key.

Download and install OpenTofu from the OpenTofu installation guide.

docs.title: Find the module files
docs.text:
The OpenTofu module is stored in this repository at:

docs/install/bootstrap-node/
├── main.tf
├── variables.tf
├── outputs.tf
├── cloud-config.tftpl
└── tofu.tfvars.example

These files are intentionally not separate navigation entries. If you cloned the repository, change to the module directory:

cd nkp-collection/docs/install/bootstrap-node

If you are reading the rendered documentation without a local clone, download all five files below and place them in the same directory:

  • main.tf
  • variables.tf
  • outputs.tf
  • cloud-config.tftpl
  • tofu.tfvars.example

Note

Do not copy only main.tf. It references variables and the cloud-config.tftpl template from the same directory.

docs.title: Configure the module
docs.text:
From the module directory:

cp tofu.tfvars.example tofu.tfvars

Edit tofu.tfvars and replace every example value.

Do not commit credentials

tofu.tfvars contains the Prism Central password and is ignored by Git. Keep it local and use your organization's secret-management process for shared automation.

docs.title: Initialize and review
docs.text:
tofu init
tofu fmt -check
tofu validate
tofu plan -var-file=tofu.tfvars

Review the plan before creating the VM.

docs.title: Create the bootstrap node
docs.text:
tofu apply -var-file=tofu.tfvars

After cloud-init completes, refresh the state and display the address:

tofu refresh -var-file=tofu.tfvars
tofu output vm_ip_address

Connect with SSH:

ssh nutanix@<bootstrap-ip>

docs.title: Option 2: Prepare a host manually
docs.text: You can use an existing Linux or macOS host. It does not have to run on Nutanix AHV. Keep it available until management-cluster creation and the Cluster API pivot have completed.

docs.title: Optional: create a Linux VM on AHV
docs.text:
In Prism Central:

  1. Create a VM from the Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image.
  2. Assign at least 4 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory, and a 100 GiB disk.
  3. Attach the VM to the bootstrap subnet.
  4. Enable DHCP or assign an address according to your network design.
  5. Add a non-root administrative user and your SSH public key with cloud-init or the image customization options.
  6. Start the VM and connect over SSH.

docs.title: Ubuntu example
docs.text:
The commands below prepare Ubuntu 24.04. Adapt the package-manager and repository steps for another Linux distribution.

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y \
  apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl git gnupg jq \
  software-properties-common unzip

Install Docker:

sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg

echo \
  "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${VERSION_CODENAME}") stable" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list >/dev/null

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io
sudo usermod -aG docker "${USER}"

Log out and reconnect so the Docker group membership takes effect.

Install kubectl 1.35:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.35/deb/Release.key \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg

echo \
  "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.35/deb/ /" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kubectl

Install yq:

sudo curl -fsSL \
  https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/latest/download/yq_linux_amd64 \
  -o /usr/local/bin/yq
sudo chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/yq

docs.title: macOS example
docs.text:
Install Docker Desktop or another compatible Linux-container runtime. With Homebrew installed:

brew install kubectl yq jq git

Start Docker and verify that Linux containers run before invoking the NKP CLI. Download the NKP CLI build that matches macOS and the Mac's CPU architecture.

For an air-gapped bootstrap node, mirror these packages and binaries internally instead of running the public download commands.

docs.title: Verify the bootstrap node
docs.text:
For either method:

docker version
kubectl version --client
yq --version
git --version
jq --version

For the OpenTofu method, check /var/log/cloud-init-output.log if provisioning is incomplete.

Field note: keep the VM until the pivot completes

Do not destroy the bootstrap VM while management-cluster creation is in progress. The temporary kind cluster contains the Cluster API controllers and conditions needed for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Remove the bootstrap node
docs.text:
After the management cluster is healthy and all required files have been copied off the VM, delete it manually or use OpenTofu:

tofu destroy -var-file=tofu.tfvars

docs.title: Create a management cluster
docs.text:
Tested with NKP 2.19.0

This guide creates a connected, self-managed NKP management cluster on Nutanix AHV using a registry mirror.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • a prepared bootstrap node;
  • Prism Central 7.5 or 7.6 and AOS 7.5 or 7.6;
  • the NKP 2.19.0 bundle;
  • a supported NKP 2.19 node image in Prism Central;
  • reserved control plane and load balancer IP addresses;
  • Prism Element, subnet, and storage container names;
  • registry mirror details.

Check before you start (NKP 2.19)

  • Kubernetes 1.36.2 is the default version. The matching node image is Rocky Linux 9.8. Use the image name exactly as it appears in Prism Central.
  • With Prism Central Projects 2.0, a cluster uses one Prism Central project for all its resources, such as VMs and volume groups. To use a user-defined project, add --pc-project=<project-name>. Omit the flag for the default project (_internal). The older --control-plane-pc-project and --worker-pc-project flags are deprecated. Prism Central, Prism Element, and AOS must be 7.6 or later for a user-defined project. The project cannot be changed after creation.

docs.title: Install the NKP CLI
docs.text:
On the bootstrap node, extract the bundle and install the CLI:

tar -xzvf nkp-bundle_v2.19.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
sudo install -m 0755 ./nkp-v2.19.0/cli/nkp /usr/local/bin/nkp
nkp version

Load the bootstrap image:

docker load --input nkp-v2.19.0/konvoy-bootstrap-image-v2.19.0.tar

docs.title: Configure the environment
docs.text:
Replace every example value:

export CLUSTER_NAME=nkp-mgmt-cluster
export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/${CLUSTER_NAME}.conf"

export NUTANIX_USER=admin
export NUTANIX_ENDPOINT=pc.example.com
export NUTANIX_PORT=9440
export NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME=PE-CLUSTER
export NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME=PRIMARY-NETWORK
export NUTANIX_STORAGE_CONTAINER_NAME=CONTAINER
export NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME=nkp-rocky-9.8-release-cis-1.36.2.qcow2

export CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP=192.0.2.10
export LB_IP_RANGE=192.0.2.11-192.0.2.20
export REGISTRY_MIRROR_URL=registry.example.com/docker.io

Read the Prism Central password without storing it in shell history:

read -r -s -p "Prism Central password: " NUTANIX_PASSWORD
export NUTANIX_PASSWORD
echo

docs.title: Create the management cluster
docs.text:
nkp create cluster nutanix -c "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --endpoint "https://${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}:${NUTANIX_PORT}" \
  --insecure \
  --control-plane-endpoint-ip "${CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP}" \
  --kubernetes-service-load-balancer-ip-range "${LB_IP_RANGE}" \
  --control-plane-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-prism-element-cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-subnets "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --worker-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --worker-prism-element-cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --worker-subnets "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --csi-storage-container "${NUTANIX_STORAGE_CONTAINER_NAME}" \
  --registry-mirror-url "https://${REGISTRY_MIRROR_URL}" \
  --skip-preflight-checks=Registry \
  --control-plane-replicas 3 \
  --control-plane-vcpus 4 \
  --control-plane-memory 16 \
  --worker-replicas 3 \
  --worker-vcpus 8 \
  --worker-memory 32 \
  --self-managed

Lab-only TLS options

--insecure and --skip-preflight-checks=Registry are appropriate only when the lab uses untrusted certificates. Configure trusted certificate authorities and remove these options in production.

docs.title: Monitor provisioning
docs.text:
While the management cluster is created:

kind get kubeconfig --name konvoy-capi-bootstrapper > bootstrap-cluster.conf
kubectl --kubeconfig bootstrap-cluster.conf get clusters,machines -A
kubectl --kubeconfig bootstrap-cluster.conf get nutanixmachines -A

Do not remove the temporary kind cluster before the pivot completes.

docs.title: Verify the management cluster
docs.text:
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" get nodes
nkp get dashboard --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}"

Log in to the NKP UI and apply the required license.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Create a workspace for the first workload cluster.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
Tested with NKP 2.19.0

A project gives an application team a consistent namespace and configuration boundary across selected clusters in one workspace.

docs.title: Configure the project
docs.text:
export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf"
export WORKSPACE_NAME=dev-workspace
export CLUSTER_NAME=nkp-dev-cluster
export PROJECT_NAME=demo-project
export PROJECT_LABEL=environment
export PROJECT_LABEL_VALUE=dev

docs.title: Create the project
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" apply -f -
apiVersion: workspaces.kommander.mesosphere.io/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: ${PROJECT_NAME}
  namespace: ${WORKSPACE_NAME}
spec:
  namespaceName: ${PROJECT_NAME}
  placement:
    clusterSelector:
      matchLabels:
        ${PROJECT_LABEL}: ${PROJECT_LABEL_VALUE}
EOF

docs.title: Assign the cluster
docs.text:
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  label cluster "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  "${PROJECT_LABEL}=${PROJECT_LABEL_VALUE}" \
  -n "${WORKSPACE_NAME}"

docs.title: Verify the project
docs.text:
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  get project "${PROJECT_NAME}" -n "${WORKSPACE_NAME}"
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  get cluster "${CLUSTER_NAME}" -n "${WORKSPACE_NAME}" --show-labels

Confirm that the project namespace appears on the selected workload cluster.

Field note: describe the cluster with labels

Prefer stable labels such as environment, region, and compliance boundary. Avoid labels that couple a cluster to only one project.

docs.title: Create a workload cluster
docs.text:
Tested with NKP 2.19.0

This guide creates an NKP-managed workload cluster on Nutanix AHV.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need a management-cluster kubeconfig, an existing workspace, a supported node image, reserved IP addresses, Nutanix infrastructure names, and registry details.

Check before you start (NKP 2.19)

  • Kubernetes 1.36.2 is the default version. The matching node image is Rocky Linux 9.8. Use the image name exactly as it appears in Prism Central.
  • With Prism Central Projects 2.0, a cluster uses one Prism Central project for all its resources, such as VMs and volume groups. To use a user-defined project, add --pc-project=<project-name>. Omit the flag for the default project (_internal). The older --control-plane-pc-project and --worker-pc-project flags are deprecated. Prism Central, Prism Element, and AOS must be 7.6 or later for a user-defined project. The project cannot be changed after creation.

docs.title: Configure the environment
docs.text:
export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf"
export WORKSPACE_NAME=dev-workspace
export CLUSTER_NAME=nkp-dev-cluster

export NUTANIX_USER=admin
export NUTANIX_ENDPOINT=pc.example.com
export NUTANIX_PORT=9440
export NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME=PE-CLUSTER
export NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME=PRIMARY-NETWORK
export NUTANIX_STORAGE_CONTAINER_NAME=CONTAINER
export NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME=nkp-rocky-9.8-release-cis-1.36.2.qcow2

export CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP=192.0.2.30
export LB_IP_RANGE=192.0.2.31-192.0.2.40
export REGISTRY_MIRROR_URL=registry.example.com/docker.io

read -r -s -p "Prism Central password: " NUTANIX_PASSWORD
export NUTANIX_PASSWORD
echo

docs.title: Create the cluster
docs.text:
nkp create cluster nutanix -c "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${WORKSPACE_NAME}" \
  --endpoint "https://${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}:${NUTANIX_PORT}" \
  --insecure \
  --control-plane-endpoint-ip "${CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT_IP}" \
  --kubernetes-service-load-balancer-ip-range "${LB_IP_RANGE}" \
  --control-plane-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-prism-element-cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-subnets "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --worker-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --worker-prism-element-cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --worker-subnets "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --csi-storage-container "${NUTANIX_STORAGE_CONTAINER_NAME}" \
  --registry-mirror-url "https://${REGISTRY_MIRROR_URL}" \
  --skip-preflight-checks=Registry \
  --control-plane-replicas 3 \
  --control-plane-vcpus 4 \
  --control-plane-memory 16 \
  --worker-replicas 3 \
  --worker-vcpus 8 \
  --worker-memory 32 \
  --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}"

Use trusted certificates and remove the insecure options in production.

docs.title: Verify the cluster
docs.text:
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  get clusters,machines -n "${WORKSPACE_NAME}"
kubectl --kubeconfig "${CLUSTER_NAME}.conf" get nodes

Field note: inspect conditions first

If provisioning stalls, describe the Cluster, Machine, and NutanixMachine resources before troubleshooting individual VMs.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Create a project for application teams.

docs.title: Create a workspace
docs.text:
Tested with NKP 2.19.0

A workspace groups clusters, platform applications, and access controls. Create it before creating the first workload cluster.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: You need a running management cluster, its kubeconfig, and permission to create workspace resources.

docs.title: Configure the workspace
docs.text:
export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf"
export WORKSPACE_NAME=dev-workspace
export WORKSPACE_DISPLAY_NAME="Development"

WORKSPACE_NAME becomes the resource name and namespace. Use a DNS-compatible name.

docs.title: Create the workspace
docs.text:
cat <<EOF | kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" apply -f -
apiVersion: workspaces.kommander.mesosphere.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workspace
metadata:
  name: ${WORKSPACE_NAME}
  annotations:
    kommander.mesosphere.io/display-name: ${WORKSPACE_DISPLAY_NAME}
spec:
  namespaceName: ${WORKSPACE_NAME}
EOF

docs.title: Verify the workspace
docs.text:
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" get workspace "${WORKSPACE_NAME}"
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" get namespace "${WORKSPACE_NAME}"

Field note: use durable boundaries

Use workspaces for long-lived ownership or governance boundaries. Use projects to organize application teams.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Create a workload cluster.

docs.title: Node images
docs.text:
Every NKP cluster node boots from an operating system image that already contains the NKP-required components: the container runtime, kubelet, Kubernetes packages, and supporting dependencies. On Nutanix AHV, that image is stored in Prism Central and referenced when you create or scale a cluster.

You have two ways to get one:

Pre-built image Custom image Source Downloaded from the Nutanix Support Portal Built by you with nkp create image nutanix Licence Starter, Pro, Ultimate Pro or Ultimate only Time to first cluster Minutes (download and upload) Longer (a build runs in Prism) Patching Nutanix publishes updated images You rebuild and roll out new images CIS Level 1 OS hardening Supported Not supported1 Extra packages, your own base configuration No Yes GPU and vGPU Ubuntu image supports GPU; Rocky image does not Yes, depending on the operating system. Supported NVIDIA drivers can be installed with --gpu-name and --vgpu-runfile FIPS Not supported Yes, with --fips, on operating systems that support it

Start with the pre-built image

Build a custom image only when you need something the pre-built image cannot give you, such as an organisation-specific base configuration, FIPS, or pre-installed drivers. A custom image is something you must rebuild and test for every Kubernetes patch release.

docs.title: How the build works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    base["Base OS image<br/>in Prism Central"]
    cli["nkp create image nutanix<br/>(runs the Image Builder container)"]
    vm["Temporary build VM<br/>in Prism Element"]
    out["NKP node image<br/>in Prism Central"]
    cluster["nkp create cluster nutanix<br/>--control-plane-vm-image<br/>--worker-vm-image"]

    base --> cli --> vm --> out --> cluster
  1. You run nkp create image nutanix from a bootstrap host with Docker or Podman. The command starts the Nutanix Image Builder (NIB) in a container.
  2. NIB creates a temporary VM in the Prism Element cluster and subnet you specify, starting from the base image.
  3. NIB installs and configures the NKP and Kubernetes components, then saves the result as a new image in Prism Central. The temporary VM exists only for the build.
  4. The command prints the new image name, for example nkp-ubuntu-24.04-1.36.2-20260101120000. Pass that name to --control-plane-vm-image and --worker-vm-image when you create a cluster.

In an air-gapped environment the build VM cannot reach OS package repositories. You first create a package bundle on an internet-connected host and carry it into the restricted network. See Build a custom image: air-gapped.

docs.title: Supported operating systems
docs.text:
Support differs by NKP release and by feature (FIPS, air-gapped, GPU, vGPU). Always confirm the exact matrix in the Nutanix documentation for your release on the Nutanix support portal.

Operating systems supported on Nutanix AHV:

Operating system Air-gapped FIPS FIPS air-gapped GPU GPU air-gapped vGPU Nutanix Image Builder Rocky Linux 9.8 Yes - - - - - Yes Ubuntu 22.04 Yes - - Yes Yes - Yes Ubuntu 24.04 Yes - - Yes Yes - Yes RHEL 8.10 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes RHEL 9.6 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes RHEL 9.8 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes

All of them support the default configuration. A dash means not applicable. Kernel versions are on the portal page.

What this means for custom builds:

  • FIPS images need RHEL.
  • GPU images need Ubuntu or RHEL. Rocky Linux does not support GPU.
  • vGPU images need RHEL.
  • Rocky Linux supports the default and air-gapped builds only.

Verify before you build

The lists above were gathered from public release information. They are not a substitute for the support matrix, which also covers kernel versions and per-feature support. Only x86-64 (AMD64) is supported.

docs.title: Where to get help
docs.text: Keep your builds close to the documented steps. For anything beyond them, such as custom Ansible roles or unusual base images, use the NKP documentation on the Nutanix support portal, ask the Nutanix Intelligent Virtual Agent (NIVA), or open a support case.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Use a pre-built image
  • Build a custom image with internet access
  • Build a custom image: air-gapped
  • Customize an image: FIPS, GPU, naming, and dry runs
  • Troubleshoot image builds

  1. In NKP 2.19, CIS Level 1 hardening is available only in the pre-built Rocky Linux and Ubuntu images. It is not a supported override for custom images. If you need CIS, use the pre-built image. ↩

docs.title: Build a custom image: air-gapped
docs.text:
In an air-gapped environment the temporary build VM cannot download operating system packages. You therefore split the work in two:

  1. On a host with internet access, create a package bundle.
  2. Move the bundle into the restricted network and build the image there.

Read Build a custom image first. The licence, base image, and Prism Central requirements are the same.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the NKP air-gapped bundle from the Nutanix Support Portal, extracted on both the connected host and the bootstrap host;
  • an internet-connected Linux or macOS AMD64 host with Docker or Podman for the package bundle step. It needs access to the operating system vendor's package repositories. Check the vendor documentation for the endpoints to allow;
  • a base image imported into Prism Central, as described in the base image requirements;
  • a bootstrap host inside the restricted network.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the package bundle (connected host)
docs.text:
tar -xzvf nkp-air-gapped-bundle_v2.19.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
cd nkp-v2.19.0
sudo install -m 0755 ./cli/nkp /usr/local/bin/nkp

docker load -i konvoy-bootstrap-image-v2.19.0.tar
docker load -i nkp-image-builder-image-v2.19.0.tar

export OS=ubuntu-24.04
export OS_BUNDLE_DIR=artifacts

nkp create package-bundle \
  --artifacts-directory "${OS_BUNDLE_DIR}" \
  "${OS}"

For a FIPS image, add --fips here and when you build the image.

The command writes the operating system packages as a .tar.gz file into OS_BUNDLE_DIR.

docs.title: Step 2: Transfer the bundle
docs.text:
Copy the contents of OS_BUNDLE_DIR into the restricted network. This is also the point to run your malware scan or approval process on the file.

You also need the base image in Prism Central, and the NKP air-gapped bundle extracted on the bootstrap host.

docs.title: Step 3: Build the image (bootstrap host)
docs.text:
Load the image builder container on the bootstrap host:

docker load -i nkp-image-builder-image-v2.19.0.tar

Set the environment:

export OS=ubuntu-24.04
export OS_BUNDLE_DIR=artifacts
export BASE_IMAGE=ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.img

export NUTANIX_ENDPOINT=pc.example.com
export NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME=PE-CLUSTER
export NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME=PRIMARY-NETWORK

export NUTANIX_USER=admin
read -r -s -p "Prism Central password: " NUTANIX_PASSWORD
export NUTANIX_PASSWORD
echo

Build:

nkp create image nutanix "${OS}" \
  --endpoint "${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}" \
  --cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --subnet "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --source-image "${BASE_IMAGE}" \
  --artifacts-directory "${OS_BUNDLE_DIR}"

--artifacts-directory tells the builder to use your local package bundle instead of fetching packages from the internet. Always provide --source-image in an air-gapped environment, because the builder cannot download a base image.

Record the printed image name in NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME and use it in the air-gapped management cluster guide.

docs.title: Optional: build through a bastion host
docs.text:
When the bootstrap host cannot reach the build VM directly, the CLI can connect through a bastion host:

nkp create image nutanix "${OS}" \
  --endpoint "${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}" \
  --cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --subnet "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --source-image "${BASE_IMAGE}" \
  --artifacts-directory "${OS_BUNDLE_DIR}" \
  --bastion-host bastion.example.com \
  --bastion-username ubuntu \
  --bastion-private-key-file "$HOME/.ssh/bastion_ed25519"

docs.title: Optional: embed container images
docs.text:
--bundle loads container image tarballs into the OS image, which can shorten first-boot time because the node does not have to pull them. Pass one or more .tar files, comma-separated:

  --bundle ./container-images/konvoy-image-bundle-v2.19.0.tar

Field note: rebuild the package bundle for every build

The package bundle reflects the repository contents on the day you created it. Create a fresh bundle when you rebuild an image for a new Kubernetes patch release, so the image and the bundle stay in step.

docs.title: Build a custom image
docs.text: This guide builds an NKP node image on Nutanix AHV from a host with internet access. For an environment without internet access, use Build a custom image: air-gapped.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • an NKP Pro or Ultimate licence. Custom images are not supported on Starter;
  • a bootstrap host with the nkp CLI and Docker or Podman. See Prepare a bootstrap node. The host must run Linux or macOS on AMD64;
  • Prism Central credentials and network access to Prism Central on port 9440;
  • a Prism Element cluster and a subnet in that cluster with DHCP or IPAM, DNS resolution, and access to the operating system's package repositories.

docs.title: Base image requirements
docs.text:
The builder starts from a base image that you import into Prism Central first. The base image must:

  • be in qcow2 or .img format;
  • boot with UEFI;
  • have a default user with sudo privileges;
  • have an SSH server installed and enabled;
  • have cloud-init installed and configured;
  • have Python 3 installed and on the path;
  • have at least 20 GB free on the root filesystem;
  • have swap disabled and a sufficiently large /var;
  • have no Kubernetes components installed.

If you build the base image from an ISO or an existing VM, apply your organisation's standard configuration first, such as NTP, DNS, certificates, and hardening, so it is already present in the base.

Do not use an NKP image as the base

Pre-built images from the Nutanix Support Portal and images created by an earlier nkp create image run cannot be used as a base image.

For the upstream cloud images, use the generic cloud image of the operating system you build. For example, ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.img for Ubuntu 24.04. Upload it to Prism Central and wait for it to become Active.

For RHEL 8.10 you must always provide a source image.

docs.title: Configure the environment
docs.text:
export OS=ubuntu-24.04
export BASE_IMAGE=ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.img

export NUTANIX_ENDPOINT=pc.example.com
export NUTANIX_PORT=9440
export NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME=PE-CLUSTER
export NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME=PRIMARY-NETWORK

export NUTANIX_USER=admin
read -r -s -p "Prism Central password: " NUTANIX_PASSWORD
export NUTANIX_PASSWORD
echo

Replace the example values. BASE_IMAGE is the name or UUID of the image you imported into Prism Central.

Choose the operating system value

The supported values for OS depend on the NKP release. List them with nkp create image nutanix --help on your CLI version, and compare with the supported operating systems.

docs.title: Run a dry run first
docs.text:
nkp create image nutanix "${OS}" \
  --endpoint "${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}" \
  --port "${NUTANIX_PORT}" \
  --cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --subnet "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --source-image "${BASE_IMAGE}" \
  --dry-run

A dry run does not keep the artifacts. It catches connection, credential, and parameter mistakes before you spend a full build on them.

Add --insecure only in a lab where Prism Central uses a certificate that the bootstrap host does not trust.

docs.title: Build the image
docs.text:
Run the same command without --dry-run:

nkp create image nutanix "${OS}" \
  --endpoint "${NUTANIX_ENDPOINT}" \
  --port "${NUTANIX_PORT}" \
  --cluster "${NUTANIX_PRISM_ELEMENT_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --subnet "${NUTANIX_SUBNET_NAME}" \
  --source-image "${BASE_IMAGE}"

The builder creates a temporary VM, configures it, and uploads the result to Prism Central. If you omit --source-image, the builder downloads the upstream base image for the operating system.

The Kubernetes version defaults to the version bundled with your CLI. Set --kubernetes-version only when you need to build for a specific version.

docs.title: Record the image name
docs.text:
When the build completes, the command prints the image name, for example:

nkp-ubuntu-24.04-1.36.2-20260101120000

Confirm the image is Active in Prism Central, then use it for cluster creation:

export NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME=nkp-ubuntu-24.04-1.36.2-20260101120000

Pass NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME to --control-plane-vm-image and --worker-vm-image in the management cluster guide.

Field note: name builds so you can find them

Use --extra-build-name to add a suffix, such as the team or a change ticket, to the image name. Several images with the same Kubernetes version are hard to tell apart in Prism Central otherwise.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Customize the build with FIPS, GPU, and naming options, or go back to Installation.

docs.title: Customize an image
docs.text:
These options extend the basic connected and air-gapped builds. Add them to the nkp create image nutanix command.

Keep it simple

Every customization is something you maintain. Use the options below, and ask Nutanix for guidance before going further. See Where to get help.

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Option Purpose --fips Build a FIPS-compliant image. Also add it to nkp create package-bundle in air-gapped builds. --gpu-name Name of a GPU in the Prism Element cluster. The builder attaches it to the temporary VM and installs the GPU drivers. --vgpu-runfile Path to the NVIDIA vGPU driver runfile to install in the image. --extra-build-name Append text to the generated image name. --kubernetes-version Build for a specific Kubernetes version instead of the CLI default. --dry-run Validate the setup without keeping artifacts. --debug Run Packer in debug mode and pause after each step. --overrides Pass an override YAML file. See Overrides.

Run nkp create image nutanix --help to see the options for your CLI version.

docs.title: FIPS
docs.text:
Add --fips to the build. For an air-gapped build, also create the package bundle with --fips. In the NKP 2.19 support matrix, FIPS images are available on RHEL only. Check the matrix for your release first.

nkp create image nutanix rhel-9.6 --fips \
  --source-image "${BASE_IMAGE}" \
  ...

docs.title: GPU and vGPU
docs.text:
GPU images are supported on Ubuntu and RHEL, not on Rocky Linux. vGPU images are supported on RHEL only. For GPU passthrough, add --gpu-name so the builder installs the driver:

nkp create image nutanix ubuntu-24.04 \
  --gpu-name "${GPU_NAME}" \
  ...

For vGPU, also pass the NVIDIA driver runfile with --vgpu-runfile. Download it from NVIDIA with your licence.

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
--overrides accepts a YAML file. It is not a general extension mechanism: it only changes variables that the selected image builder already uses. Keys it does not know are ignored, and it does not run scripts.

Two uses are straightforward.

Build-time proxy. The proxy is used while the image builds and is not left in the finished image.

proxy.yaml
http_proxy: http://proxy.example.com:8080
https_proxy: http://proxy.example.com:8080
no_proxy: localhost,127.0.0.1,.cluster.local

nkp create image nutanix "${OS}" \
  ... \
  --overrides proxy.yaml

Extra operating system packages.

packages.yaml
packages:
  extra_packages:
    - make
    - pkg-config

In an air-gapped build, pass the file when you create the package bundle so the packages are included in it:

nkp create package-bundle \
  --artifacts-directory "${OS_BUNDLE_DIR}" \
  --overrides packages.yaml \
  "${OS}"

For anything else, ask Nutanix first. The portal documents custom overrides as something to discuss with Nutanix Support.

docs.title: What custom images do not cover
docs.text:
These are not generic override keys, and adding them to a YAML file has no effect:

You want Do this instead CIS Level 1 hardening Use the pre-built Rocky Linux or Ubuntu image. NTP servers Configure them when you create the cluster, or in your base image. A corporate CA in the node trust store Install it in the base image before the build. Extra kernel parameters Apply them in the base image, and confirm with Nutanix that the change is supported. Registry CA and credentials Use cluster creation options such as --registry-mirror-cacert. Do not bake credentials into an image.

--additional-trust-bundle is not a node trust store

In NKP 2.18 the option covers Prism Central certificate validation. It does not add a CA to the operating system of cluster nodes.

If the builder itself must trust a TLS-inspecting proxy, configure that trust on the machine that runs the builder. It is separate from what ends up in the image.

docs.title: Dry run and debug
docs.text: Use --dry-run while you develop a build. Use --debug when a build fails and you want to see each step. Run --debug in an interactive terminal, because it waits for you after every step.

docs.title: Treat images like releases
docs.text: Record the NKP CLI version, the exact command, the base image name, the package bundle, and the resulting image name. When Kubernetes moves to a new version, rebuild the image and roll it out.

docs.title: Use a pre-built image
docs.text: Nutanix publishes ready-to-use node images for AHV. They are the quickest way to a working cluster and are available on every NKP licence tier.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • access to the Nutanix Support Portal;
  • Prism Central access with permission to upload images;
  • a licence for NKP Starter, Pro, or Ultimate.

Pre-built images are published for Rocky Linux and Ubuntu. Starter customers use the Rocky Linux image. Pro and Ultimate customers can also use the Ubuntu image.

docs.title: Download the image
docs.text:
1. Open the NKP download page on the Nutanix Support Portal.
  2. In the product drop-down at the top of the page, change NKP to NKP Operating System Images.
  3. Select the NKP version you run or plan to upgrade to.
  4. Download the image for your operating system.

Do not rename the file

NKP refers to the image by name. Keep the filename exactly as downloaded when you upload it to Prism Central.

docs.title: Upload to Prism Central
docs.text: Upload the file with the Prism Central image import workflow, or with the API or OpenTofu if you automate Prism. Wait until the image state is Active.

docs.title: Use it when creating a cluster
docs.text:
Record the image name and pass it to the cluster creation command:

export NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME=nkp-rocky-9.8-release-cis-1.36.2.qcow2

nkp create cluster nutanix -c "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --control-plane-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  --worker-vm-image "${NUTANIX_MACHINE_TEMPLATE_IMAGE_NAME}" \
  ...

The remaining flags are in the management cluster guide.

What you get

The pre-built operating system layer is hardened to CIS Level 1, and the NKP and Kubernetes components follow CIS Level 2 guidance. Custom images are not CIS-hardened by the standard build.

docs.title: When to build your own instead
docs.text:
Build a custom image if you need FIPS, your own base configuration or agents, or GPU drivers on an operating system whose pre-built image does not include them.

Pre-built images cannot be a base image

You cannot use a downloaded pre-built image, or an image produced by an earlier NIB build, as the base image for a new build. Start from an upstream cloud image or an image you built from an ISO.

docs.title: Troubleshoot image builds
docs.text: This page lists the checks that resolve most failed builds. It is general guidance based on how the builder works. It does not replace the Nutanix documentation or a support case.

docs.title: Before you rerun a build
docs.text:
1. Run the same command with --dry-run to separate connection problems from build problems.
  2. Check Prism Central for a leftover temporary VM from the failed run, and for a partial image. Remove them if they are no longer needed.
  3. Rerun with --debug in an interactive terminal to stop after each step.

docs.title: Common causes
docs.text: Symptom Check Cannot connect to Prism Central Endpoint format (host, host:port, or URL), port 9440, credentials, and whether the certificate is trusted. Use --insecure only in labs. Build VM never gets an address The subnet must belong to the selected Prism Element cluster and provide DHCP or IPAM. Build VM boots but the builder cannot connect The bootstrap host must reach the VM's subnet. Use a bastion host with --bastion-* when it cannot. Package download fails (connected build) DNS resolution and access to the operating system's package repositories from the build VM. Package install fails (air-gapped build) --artifacts-directory points at the package bundle, and the bundle was created for the same operating system, Kubernetes version, and FIPS setting. Base image rejected or build fails early Verify the base image requirements: UEFI, sudo user, SSH, cloud-init, Python 3, 20 GB free, no Kubernetes packages. Build fails with a pre-built image as the base Use an upstream cloud image or an ISO-based image instead. NKP images cannot be a base. Image builder container not found In air-gapped mode, run docker load for the nkp-image-builder image from the NKP bundle. Cluster creation cannot find the image The name passed to --control-plane-vm-image and --worker-vm-image must match the image name in Prism Central exactly.

docs.title: Escalate with the right information
docs.text:
Ask the Nutanix Intelligent Virtual Agent (NIVA) or search the NKP documentation on the support portal first. If the problem remains, open a support case and include:

  • the NKP CLI version (nkp version) and the full command, without passwords;
  • the operating system and base image name;
  • whether the build is air-gapped and whether --fips, GPU, or --overrides were used;
  • the terminal output of the failed run, including --debug output if you have it.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
Inference is the use of a trained model to produce a result. For a large language model (LLM), an application sends a prompt to an inference endpoint and receives generated tokens.

Kubernetes does not perform inference. It schedules and operates the model servers, gateways, storage integrations, and supporting services that do.

docs.title: The request path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    app["Application"] --> gateway["AI gateway"]
    gateway --> endpoint["Inference endpoint"]
    endpoint --> runtime["Model runtime"]
    runtime --> gpu["GPU"]
    runtime --> storage["Models, data, and cache"]

Each layer has a different responsibility:

  • The application sends prompts and consumes responses.
  • The AI gateway applies routing, authentication, limits, and policy.
  • The inference endpoint provides a stable API for a model service.
  • The model runtime loads the model and executes inference.
  • The GPU performs accelerated computation.
  • Storage supplies model artifacts, data, and persistent or shared state.

docs.title: Model, runtime, and endpoint
docs.text:
A model is a set of learned parameters and its associated metadata. Model weights can consume many gigabytes of storage and GPU memory.

An inference runtime is software such as NVIDIA NIM or vLLM that loads a model and serves requests.

An endpoint is the API exposed to applications. Several runtime replicas can serve one logical endpoint.

Keeping these concepts separate lets platform teams change a runtime, model version, or replica count without changing every application.

docs.title: Tokens and context
docs.text:
LLMs process text as tokens, not characters or words. Usage, throughput, and limits are commonly measured in tokens.

The context window is the token content available to a model for one request. It includes the prompt, system instructions, retrieved information, tool results, and generated output.

Larger context can increase memory consumption and time to first token. Sending all available information is not automatically better than selecting relevant context.

docs.title: KV cache
docs.text:
During generation, transformer runtimes store attention data in a key-value (KV) cache. Reusing this data avoids recomputing earlier tokens.

KV cache consumes valuable GPU memory. Some architectures can place cache tiers in CPU memory or shared storage. This can support longer contexts or more concurrent requests, but adds a data path that must meet latency and throughput requirements.

docs.title: Time to first token
docs.text: Time to first token measures how long a user waits before generation begins. It is affected by queueing, model loading, prompt length, cache state, storage, and runtime behavior.

docs.title: Inter-token latency
docs.text: Inter-token latency measures the delay between generated tokens. It influences the perceived speed of streamed responses.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: Throughput measures tokens or requests served over time. Optimizing throughput can conflict with minimizing latency for an individual request.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Concurrency is the number of requests processed at the same time. GPU memory, batching, context length, and runtime configuration constrain it.

Measure these signals together. GPU utilization alone does not describe the user experience.

docs.title: Batching and scaling
docs.text:
Inference runtimes can combine several requests into a batch to use the GPU more efficiently. Larger batches can improve total throughput but may increase queueing latency.

Scaling has two levels:

  • Model-server scaling: add or remove inference replicas.
  • Cluster scaling: add or remove GPU-capable nodes.

Adding pods does not help when no GPU capacity is available. Adding GPU nodes does not help when model replicas, quotas, or routing remain unchanged.

docs.title: Why an AI gateway is different
docs.text:
A traditional load balancer routes network requests. An AI gateway can also understand model- and provider-specific concerns:

  • route by model name or policy;
  • select private or external providers;
  • authenticate applications and upstream providers;
  • limit requests or token usage;
  • provide failover;
  • collect model, latency, and usage telemetry.

Envoy AI Gateway is one open source, Kubernetes-native option. Nutanix Enterprise AI provides an integrated Nutanix experience for model and endpoint management.

docs.title: RAG and vector search
docs.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds selected enterprise information to a prompt:

  1. Content is ingested and divided into useful chunks.
  2. An embedding model converts content into vectors.
  3. A vector database finds content related to a query.
  4. The selected content is added to the model context.
  5. The inference runtime generates a response.

RAG does not train the foundation model. It supplies relevant context at request time. Its quality depends on ingestion, chunking, metadata, retrieval, access control, and data freshness.

docs.title: Why storage matters
docs.text:
Inference platforms need storage for:

  • model weights and runtime artifacts;
  • RAG source data and vector indexes;
  • shared caches;
  • pipeline and evaluation artifacts;
  • logs, backups, and application state.

Model startup can be limited by how quickly weights reach the runtime. RAG can be limited by retrieval latency. Shared cache designs can be limited by network and storage throughput.

Choose block, file, or object services based on the access pattern. Do not select storage only by capacity.

docs.title: The role of Kubernetes
docs.text:
Kubernetes contributes:

  • GPU-aware scheduling and node selection;
  • health probes and replacement of failed replicas;
  • services and gateway integration;
  • declarative configuration and secrets;
  • persistent storage through CSI;
  • controlled rollouts;
  • metrics and logs;
  • namespaces, quotas, and policy.

Kubernetes does not decide which model is accurate, how much GPU memory it needs, or whether the inference design meets latency targets. Those require model- and workload-specific validation.

Field note: test cold and warm behavior

Test a cold model start as well as a warm steady state. Local caches can make a demonstration look fast while hiding the model-distribution and storage behavior that determines recovery and scale-out time.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
Cloud native describes an operating model, not a location. A workload does not become cloud native merely because it runs in a container or public cloud.

Cloud native systems use APIs, declared desired state, automation, replaceable components, and observable behavior to operate reliably at scale.

docs.title: Why this matters for NKP
docs.text:
NKP is built around controllers. Cluster API, Kubernetes, and Flux continuously compare desired state with actual state and reconcile differences.

This makes the platform repeatable, but only when teams change the declared source instead of bypassing it with manual fixes.

flowchart LR
    source["Declared source<br/>Git · Kubernetes API"] --> controller["Controller"]
    controller --> system["Running system"]
    system --> observation["Status and conditions"]
    observation --> controller

docs.title: Declare the outcome
docs.text:
Describe what should exist: the cluster version, replica count, application release, policy, or storage request. Let controllers determine the actions required to reach that state.

This is different from a runbook containing only a sequence of imperative steps. The declared state remains after the command has finished.

docs.title: Reconcile continuously
docs.text:
Controllers do not run once. They continue to observe the system. If actual state drifts, they act again.

Operational questions therefore include:

  • Which controller owns this resource?
  • Where is its desired state stored?
  • Which condition prevents reconciliation?

docs.title: Prefer replacement over hidden change
docs.text:
Build a new container or node image rather than making undocumented changes to a running instance. Replacement creates a repeatable path for scaling and recovery.

Not every component can be replaced without planning. Databases and other stateful systems need stable identity, storage, replication, and backup.

docs.title: Design for failure
docs.text: Assume that pods, nodes, networks, and dependencies can fail. Availability comes from replicas, failure domains, health checks, controlled disruption, and tested recovery—not from assuming an individual instance will remain healthy.

docs.title: Expose health and behavior
docs.text:
The platform needs signals it can act on:

  • readiness: can this instance receive traffic?
  • liveness: should this instance be restarted?
  • startup: has slow initialization completed?
  • metrics, logs, and traces: what is the system doing?
  • Kubernetes conditions and events: why is reconciliation blocked?

Monitoring only CPU and memory is not enough to understand an application.

docs.title: Automate through APIs
docs.text: Kubernetes resources, Cluster API objects, Flux resources, and CI/CD systems provide automation interfaces. Prefer these stable APIs over UI-only procedures or manual changes that cannot be reviewed and repeated.

docs.title: What cloud native does not mean
docs.text:
Cloud native does not automatically provide:

  • application high availability;
  • correct resource sizing;
  • persistent data protection;
  • secure network policy;
  • zero-downtime upgrades;
  • useful observability;
  • lower cost.

The platform provides mechanisms. Application and platform teams must choose and validate the design.

docs.title: Shared responsibility
docs.text:
Infrastructure teams provide reliable compute, network, storage, identity, and failure domains.

Platform teams provide Kubernetes clusters, policies, platform services, upgrade paths, and developer interfaces.

Application teams provide healthy containers, resource requests, probes, scaling behavior, data consistency, and application-level telemetry.

Unclear ownership between these groups is a larger operational risk than many individual technology choices.

Field note: automate the second occurrence

A manual investigation can be appropriate while learning. If the same change or recovery action is needed again, move it into declared configuration, policy, or automation.

docs.title: Deep dive: pets and cattle is incomplete
docs.text:
The common “pets versus cattle” analogy helps explain replaceable compute, but it can hide important state. A better distinction is:

  • reconstructable state: images, manifests, policies, and configuration held in a trusted source;
  • persistent business state: databases, object data, model artifacts, and secrets that need protection;
  • runtime state: pods, caches, and temporary resources that can be recreated.

Design recovery for each category instead of labeling an entire system disposable.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
A Kubernetes workload is not a smaller virtual machine. Kubernetes assumes that application instances can be recreated, rescheduled, and scaled from declared configuration. The platform continuously reconciles this desired state.

Virtual machines remain important: NKP commonly runs Kubernetes nodes as VMs on Nutanix AHV. What changes is how applications above those nodes are operated.

docs.title: The key shift
docs.text:
Traditional infrastructure operations often focus on preserving and repairing a specific server. Kubernetes focuses on maintaining the required application state, even when individual instances disappear.

flowchart LR
    desired["Desired state<br/>3 replicas"] --> controller["Kubernetes controller"]
    controller --> actual["Actual state<br/>2 healthy replicas"]
    controller --> replacement["Create replacement replica"]

This does not mean that everything is disposable. Data, identity, policy, and declared configuration still require protection. The replaceable part is the application instance, not the business state it serves.

docs.title: Familiar concepts and where the analogy breaks
A pod is not a VM
docs.text:
A pod is the smallest Kubernetes scheduling unit. It contains one or more containers that share networking and storage context.

A pod normally:

  • has no expectation of a permanent name or IP address;
  • is created by a higher-level controller;
  • can be replaced on another node;
  • receives configuration and storage through Kubernetes resources.

Do not administer pods as long-lived servers. Change the owning Deployment, StatefulSet, Helm release, or Git source.

docs.title: A container image is not a fully managed VM template
docs.text:
Both package software for repeatable deployment, but a container image normally contains the application and its runtime dependencies—not a complete operating system to patch and administer.

Build a new image for an application change. Do not log into a running container and treat the modification as persistent configuration.

docs.title: A Kubernetes node is closer to a VM
docs.text:
A node supplies CPU, memory, networking, and local resources to pods. On NKP, a node is commonly an AHV virtual machine created from a supported node image.

Node maintenance still matters, but Cluster API can replace nodes through a rolling lifecycle instead of requiring every node to be repaired indefinitely.

docs.title: A Service is not the application instance
docs.text:
A Kubernetes Service gives clients a stable network identity while the pods behind it change. Ingress or Gateway API resources provide application-level routing from outside the cluster.

Do not configure consumers with individual pod IP addresses.

docs.title: A PersistentVolume is not simply a virtual disk
docs.text:
A workload requests storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim. A StorageClass describes how storage is provisioned. CSI connects that request to the storage system.

The application still owns data consistency. Attaching persistent storage does not automatically make an application highly available or safely backed up.

docs.title: A namespace is not a resource pool or VLAN
docs.text:
A namespace scopes names, access, quotas, and policy within a cluster. It is not an infrastructure isolation boundary by itself.

Strong multi-tenancy may also require network policy, admission policy, dedicated nodes, or separate clusters.

Putting worker node pools into different VLANs does not automatically place or isolate namespaces there. Kubernetes can reschedule pods between eligible nodes, and the CNI provides the pod network across the cluster. See Worker VLANs.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Traditional approach: change the running system.

Cloud native approach: change the declared source and let a controller reconcile the system.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Traditional approach: add CPU and memory to one server.

Cloud native approach: add replicas where the application supports horizontal scaling, then scale nodes when the cluster needs more capacity.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Traditional approach: restore or repair the failed server.

Cloud native approach: replace failed application instances and nodes from known configuration, then restore persistent state when required.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
Traditional approach: patch a server in place.

Cloud native approach: roll out a new image or declared version while controllers maintain the required availability.

docs.title: Stable endpoints, replaceable nodes
docs.text:
A common infrastructure instinct is to assign every Kubernetes node a permanent IP address. That makes sense when a server is a long-lived identity. It conflicts with the CAPI model, where a node is one replaceable instance of a declared Machine.

During repair, scaling, or an upgrade, CAPI can:

  1. create a new VM from the declared image and machine template;
  2. obtain an address from infrastructure IPAM or DHCP;
  3. join the new node to Kubernetes;
  4. drain and remove the old node.

The replacement does not need the old node's address. Stable access belongs at other layers:

  • the Kubernetes API uses a reserved control plane endpoint;
  • applications use Services and DNS rather than node addresses;
  • external traffic uses load balancer or ingress addresses;
  • persistent data uses storage abstractions rather than node-local identity.

Dynamic assignment does not mean unmanaged addressing. The subnet, IP pool, routes, DNS, firewall rules, and reserved endpoint ranges still require deliberate design. Prefer subnet- or role-based policy over allowlists tied to individual node addresses.

Pre-provisioned clusters are different: NKP receives an inventory of existing hosts and their addresses. Use that model when physical machines, an external provisioning system, or fixed host identities are genuine requirements. On Nutanix AHV, the normal CAPX workflow provides more lifecycle automation by creating replaceable VMs and using Nutanix IPAM or DHCP.

Cluster API Provider Pre-Provisioned (CAPPP) still provides CAPI-based Kubernetes lifecycle operations. It stops at the host boundary: another system or team must provision, repair, replace, and decommission the machines in its inventory. CAPX extends reconciliation across that boundary and manages the AHV VMs as well.

docs.title: What still matters from infrastructure engineering
docs.text:
Cloud native platforms still depend on strong infrastructure practice:

  • capacity and failure-domain design;
  • IP address management, DNS, NTP, and certificates;
  • storage performance, availability, and data protection;
  • network latency, bandwidth, and security boundaries;
  • hardware and hypervisor lifecycle;
  • disaster recovery and operational ownership.

The goal is not to discard infrastructure expertise. It is to apply that expertise to a controller-driven system.

Field note: ask what should survive

For every workload, identify which parts are replaceable and which state must survive. This question prevents both extremes: treating every pod like a permanent VM and treating important data as disposable.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Short definitions for terms used throughout these field docs.

AI gateway A traffic and policy layer in front of model endpoints. It can provide routing, authentication, usage limits, failover, and AI-specific telemetry. Air-gapped An environment that cannot access external networks. Required artifacts must be transferred in and served from internal systems. Attached cluster A Kubernetes cluster created outside NKP and connected for supported management services. NKP does not own its infrastructure lifecycle. CAPX Cluster API Provider Nutanix. The controller that translates Cluster API resources into operations on Nutanix infrastructure. Cilium The default NKP Container Network Interface implementation. It uses eBPF for networking, service handling, and network policy. Cloud native An operating model based on APIs, declared state, automation, reconciliation, replaceable components, and observable systems. It does not mean only public cloud. Cluster API (CAPI) An upstream Kubernetes project that represents Kubernetes clusters and machines as declarative API resources. CNI Container Network Interface. A standard used to connect pods to the cluster network. Container An isolated application process packaged with its runtime dependencies. A container is not a complete virtual machine. Container image An immutable package used to create containers. Controller Software that watches desired and actual state and takes action to reconcile them. CSI Container Storage Interface. A standard that connects Kubernetes storage requests to storage systems. D2iQ The company name adopted by Mesosphere in 2019. Its D2iQ Kubernetes Platform technology later evolved into NKP after joining Nutanix. Desired state The declared configuration that controllers attempt to maintain. Deployment A Kubernetes workload controller commonly used for stateless replicated applications and rolling updates. Envoy AI Gateway An open source project built on Envoy Proxy and Kubernetes Gateway API for routing and governing generative AI traffic. Flux An open source GitOps toolkit that reconciles Kubernetes resources from declared sources such as Git, Helm, and OCI repositories. GitOps An operating practice in which version-controlled, declarative configuration is reconciled automatically into a running system. GPU node A Kubernetes node with GPU resources and the software required to advertise them to the scheduler. Helm A Kubernetes application packaging and release-management tool. Inference Using a trained model to generate a prediction, classification, embedding, or response. Inference endpoint A stable API through which applications send inference requests. Inference runtime Software that loads a model and serves inference requests, such as NVIDIA NIM or vLLM. Kommander The NKP multi-cluster management layer that runs on the management cluster. Konvoy The historical product and component name associated with Kubernetes cluster creation, runtime, node images, and lifecycle operations. Kubeconfig A file containing Kubernetes cluster connection, identity, and context information used by tools such as kubectl. Kubernetes node A physical or virtual machine that runs pods. On Nutanix AHV, NKP nodes are commonly virtual machines. KV cache Key-value attention data retained by an LLM runtime to avoid recomputing earlier tokens during generation. Large language model (LLM) A model trained to process and generate language represented as tokens. Managed cluster A workload cluster whose infrastructure lifecycle is controlled by NKP through Cluster API. Management cluster The NKP cluster that hosts fleet-management, application, and Cluster API controllers. Mesosphere The original company name behind technology that later became D2iQ and then formed part of NKP. Mindthegap An open source utility for creating and importing OCI image bundles in air-gapped environments. Namespace A Kubernetes scope for resource names, access control, quota, and policy inside one cluster. NKP Nutanix Kubernetes Platform. Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI) A Nutanix product for deploying, managing, and governing AI models and inference endpoints on supported Kubernetes environments. OCI Open Container Initiative. It defines standards used for container image formats, runtimes, and distribution. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) A Kubernetes workload's request for persistent storage. Pod The smallest Kubernetes scheduling unit. It contains one or more containers that share networking and storage context. Prism Central The Nutanix management plane used by CAPX to provision and manage resources on Nutanix infrastructure. Project An NKP application-team boundary that provides a namespace and configuration scope across selected clusters in one workspace. RAG Retrieval-augmented generation. A pattern that retrieves relevant information and adds it to a model's context at inference time. Reconciliation The repeated process of comparing desired state with actual state and acting to reduce the difference. Replica One running instance of a workload managed as part of a desired count. Service A Kubernetes resource that gives a changing group of pods a stable network address and DNS name. StorageClass A Kubernetes resource that describes how a class of persistent storage is provisioned. Token A unit of text processed or generated by a language model. A token is not always a complete word. Vector database A system optimized to store embeddings and find vectors similar to a query. Workspace An NKP boundary that groups clusters, administration, access controls, and platform applications. Workload cluster A Kubernetes cluster intended primarily to run application workloads rather than NKP fleet-management services.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
Kubernetes runs containerized workloads across a group of nodes. Users submit desired state to the Kubernetes API. Controllers schedule workloads, maintain replicas, connect services, and report status.

The Kubernetes API—not an individual node—is the main operational interface.

docs.title: The cluster
docs.text:
A Kubernetes cluster has two main parts:

  • The control plane stores desired state and runs the API server, scheduler, and controllers.
  • Worker nodes run application pods through the kubelet and container runtime.
flowchart LR
    user["kubectl, GitOps, or API client"] --> api["Kubernetes API"]
    api --> controllers["Scheduler and controllers"]
    controllers --> nodes["Worker nodes"]
    nodes --> pods["Pods"]

On NKP, Cluster API manages the VMs and Kubernetes lifecycle around this cluster. Kubernetes then manages workloads inside it.

docs.title: Pod
docs.text: A Pod contains one or more containers that must run together. Pods are replaceable runtime instances and are normally created by another controller.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: A Deployment manages stateless pod replicas and rolling updates. Change the deployment template or its source rather than editing its pods.

docs.title: StatefulSet
docs.text: A StatefulSet provides stable ordering and identity for workloads that require them. It does not make the application data consistent automatically.

docs.title: DaemonSet
docs.text: A DaemonSet runs a pod on each matching node. Networking, logging, storage, and security agents commonly use this pattern.

docs.title: Job and CronJob
docs.text: A Job runs work to completion. A CronJob creates jobs on a schedule.

docs.title: Service
docs.text: A Service gives a changing group of pods a stable virtual address and DNS name. Clients connect to the service instead of individual pod IP addresses.

docs.title: Ingress and Gateway API
docs.text: Ingress and Gateway API resources route application traffic into or within the cluster. A controller implements the requested routing on a proxy or load balancer.

docs.title: NetworkPolicy
docs.text: A NetworkPolicy declares which network connections are permitted. Enforcement depends on the cluster's CNI implementation.

docs.title: ConfigMap
docs.text: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration for workloads.

docs.title: Secret
docs.text: A Secret stores sensitive values in the Kubernetes API. It still requires appropriate encryption, access control, rotation, and often integration with an external secret-management system.

docs.title: ServiceAccount
docs.text: A ServiceAccount gives a workload an identity for Kubernetes API access. Role-based access control determines what that identity may do.

docs.title: Storage objects
docs.text:
A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage. A StorageClass selects the provisioning behavior. A CSI driver translates the request into storage-system operations.

Deleting a pod does not delete its persistent volume by default, but reclaim policy and application behavior must be understood before relying on this for data protection.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text: Resource requests describe the CPU and memory a workload needs for scheduling. The scheduler uses requests to select a node.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limits constrain usage. A container that exceeds its memory limit can be terminated. CPU limits can throttle a workload.

Missing or unrealistic requests make cluster capacity and scheduling behavior unpredictable.

docs.title: Probes
docs.text:
• A readiness probe controls whether an instance receives traffic.
  • A liveness probe tells Kubernetes when to restart an unhealthy instance.
  • A startup probe protects slow-starting applications from premature liveness failures.

docs.title: Namespaces and clusters
docs.text:
Namespaces organize resources inside one cluster. Separate clusters provide a stronger boundary for lifecycle, failure, upgrades, and administration.

Use a namespace when teams can safely share the cluster. Use separate clusters when requirements demand independent lifecycle, failure domains, versions, or stronger isolation.

See Multi-tenancy for shared-cluster, dedicated-cluster, and NKP organizational patterns.

Field note: start with owner references

When troubleshooting a pod, inspect its owner references. Move upward from the pod to its ReplicaSet, Deployment, Helm release, or Flux resource until you find the declared source that should be changed.

docs.title: Useful inspection commands
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
kubectl get events -n <namespace> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl api-resources

These commands inspect state. They do not replace understanding the controller that owns the resource.
