docs.title: In one minute
docs.text: Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP) creates and manages Kubernetes clusters. A management cluster acts as the control point for a fleet of workload clusters. NKP uses upstream projects such as Kubernetes, Cluster API, Flux, Cilium, and CSI instead of introducing a separate proprietary workload API.

docs.title: What NKP manages
docs.text:
NKP brings four concerns together:

  • Cluster lifecycle: create, scale, upgrade, and delete Kubernetes clusters.
  • Fleet organization: group clusters into workspaces and give teams projects.
  • Platform services: deploy monitoring, logging, backup, policy, and other applications consistently.
  • Infrastructure integration: connect Kubernetes networking, storage, and compute to Nutanix or another supported environment.

docs.title: The fleet model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    team["Platform team"] --> management["Management cluster"]
    management --> managed["Managed workload clusters"]
    management -.-> attached["Attached clusters"]
    projects["Workspaces and projects"] --> management

The management cluster runs Kommander and lifecycle controllers.

A managed cluster is created through NKP. NKP owns its infrastructure lifecycle through Cluster API.

An attached cluster is created elsewhere. NKP can provide supported management services without taking ownership of its infrastructure lifecycle.

docs.title: The organizational model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    global["Global"] --> workspace["Workspace"]
    workspace --> clusters["Clusters"]
    workspace --> project["Project"]
    project --> namespaces["Namespaces on selected clusters"]
  • A workspace is a durable cluster and administration boundary.
  • A project gives an application team a namespace and configuration boundary across selected clusters.

Workspaces are not folders for individual applications. Projects provide that application-team scope.

docs.title: The reconciliation model
docs.text:
NKP stores desired state and uses controllers to make reality match it:

  • Cluster API reconciles cluster infrastructure.
  • Flux reconciles platform and catalog applications.
  • Kubernetes controllers reconcile workloads and services.

If someone manually changes a generated object, a controller may change it back. The correct fix is usually to update the declared source.

docs.title: The infrastructure relationship
docs.text:
Kubernetes does not replace infrastructure. It consumes infrastructure through standard interfaces:

  • CNI for pod networking;
  • CSI for persistent storage;
  • OCI for container images;
  • infrastructure providers such as CAPX for virtual machines and networks.

Nutanix supplies compute, network integration, and data services. NKP supplies the Kubernetes and fleet operating model above them.

Field note: find the owning controller

Before changing an object, determine which controller owns it and where its desired configuration is stored. Editing the generated object often fixes only the symptom until the next reconciliation.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
• New to the operating model? Read Cloud native for system engineers.
  • New to Kubernetes objects? Read Kubernetes fundamentals.
  • Ready for detail? Open the Architecture overview.

docs.title: Does the bootstrap node have to run Ubuntu?
docs.text:
No. The bootstrap node is an execution host for the NKP CLI, Docker, and a temporary kind cluster. It can be a compatible Linux machine, Linux VM, or macOS workstation. Ubuntu is used by the included OpenTofu example.

Match the NKP CLI and container images to the host operating system and CPU architecture. Check release support before using an ARM or Apple Silicon host.

docs.title: What is the difference between Konvoy and Kommander?
docs.text:
Konvoy is the historical name associated with Kubernetes cluster creation, node images, runtime, and lifecycle operations.

Kommander is the multi-cluster management layer. It provides workspaces, projects, platform applications, fleet views, and the management UI.

Both names remain in current commands, images, namespaces, and logs. See Structure and history.

docs.title: Why do current NKP resources use mesosphere.io or d2iq.io?
docs.text:
Kubernetes API-group names are stable identifiers. Renaming them when the company or product name changes would require disruptive API and data migrations. Legacy-looking domains can therefore identify current, supported resources.

Do not change an apiVersion merely to make it use a Nutanix domain.

docs.title: Should application workloads run on the management cluster?
docs.text: Normally, no. The management cluster should be reserved for NKP controllers, fleet services, and platform administration. Run business applications on managed or attached workload clusters.

docs.title: Do Kubernetes nodes need static IP addresses?
docs.text:
Normally, no. With nkp create cluster nutanix, CAPX creates and replaces node VMs while Nutanix IPAM or DHCP assigns their addresses. The NKP CLI does not expose flags for assigning a fixed address to each Nutanix node.

This is intentional. A Machine is replaceable infrastructure: when CAPI repairs, scales, or upgrades a cluster, it can create a new VM with a new address and remove the old one. Kubernetes Services, DNS, and the control plane endpoint provide stable access above those changing nodes.

Do reserve static addresses for:

  • the Kubernetes control plane endpoint;
  • service LoadBalancer address ranges;
  • ingress or other explicitly designed external endpoints.

Those addresses must be outside DHCP or Nutanix IPAM pools to prevent conflicts.

If an organization requires already-created hosts with fixed addresses, nkp create cluster preprovisioned accepts an inventory of those hosts and connects to them over SSH. This is not a static-IP option for CAPX-created AHV VMs: the organization becomes responsible for provisioning, addressing, and maintaining the host inventory.

The pre-provisioned provider still uses CAPI and supports NKP lifecycle operations for Kubernetes, the control plane, and core add-ons. It does not create, repair, or delete the underlying hosts. Scaling or replacing capacity therefore requires suitable hosts to be added to the external inventory.

Use pre-provisioned infrastructure because the environment requires existing hosts—not only to make replaceable nodes look like traditional permanent VMs. See From VMs to Kubernetes.

docs.title: Should Kubernetes workers be placed in different VLANs?
docs.text:
Not by default. A routed multi-subnet cluster can work, but VLANs are normally the wrong boundary for applications or NKP projects.

A VLAN is attached to a worker VM. Pods are scheduled and rescheduled across eligible workers, so a namespace does not stay in one VLAN unless additional scheduling rules dedicate nodes to it. Even then, taints and affinity control placement—not network traffic.

For shared clusters, use:

  • NetworkPolicy for pod and namespace traffic;
  • RBAC for API access;
  • quotas for shared capacity;
  • workload policy for pod security;
  • dedicated node pools only where hardware or capacity separation is required.

Use a dedicated workload cluster when a tenant needs a physical network or stronger security boundary.

NKP can select a Nutanix subnet for a worker node pool with nkp create nodepool nutanix --subnets. Use this for a validated infrastructure requirement, not to recreate a VLAN-per-application VM design. All worker subnets must provide the connectivity required by the selected CNI, Kubernetes control plane, storage, registries, and platform services.

See Worker VLANs for design and validation guidance.

docs.title: Can one management cluster manage multiple Prism Element clusters?
docs.text:
Yes. A management cluster can manage workload clusters on multiple Prism Element clusters. Multi-Prism Central and mixed-provider designs depend on the NKP edition and release.

NKP can also use supported Prism Element failure domains to distribute one cluster's nodes. Validate networking, storage topology, latency, licensing, and the compatibility matrix before implementing that pattern.

See Availability and recovery.

docs.title: What happens when the management cluster is unavailable?
docs.text:
Existing workload clusters and applications continue running. Central lifecycle and fleet operations are affected, including cluster creation, scaling, upgrades, the Kommander UI, and centralized authentication or reconciliation services.

Keep protected administrative kubeconfigs and a tested management-plane recovery procedure.

docs.title: What is the difference between standard and air-gapped installs?
docs.text:
• Standard uses the normal connected or registry-mirrored workflow.
  • Air-gapped transfers all required bundles, node images, packages, and registry content into a disconnected environment.

Both use the default Cilium CNI. Nutanix Flow CNI is an option that replaces Cilium and requires a modified cluster manifest. It is not covered in these guides.

Choose the path and the CNI before cluster creation. Retrofitting a different CNI into a running cluster is disruptive.

docs.title: Does an air-gapped installation require an external registry?
docs.text:
Not always. NKP supports a built-in infrastructure registry workflow as well as an external enterprise registry. An external registry is useful when an organization already operates Harbor, Artifactory, Nexus, or another supported registry as a shared service.

See Air-gapped deployment.

docs.title: Why is a cluster stuck while its VMs appear healthy?
docs.text:
VM power state is only one part of Cluster API reconciliation. Start with the Kubernetes conditions and events:

kubectl get clusters,machines -A
kubectl get kubeadmcontrolplanes,machinedeployments -A
kubectl describe cluster <cluster-name> -n <namespace>
kubectl get events -n <namespace> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Then inspect NutanixCluster, NutanixMachine, and controller logs. The first failed condition usually identifies whether the problem is infrastructure, bootstrap, networking, or control plane readiness.

docs.title: How do I remove a failed management-cluster installation?
docs.text:
First collect a support bundle with nkp diagnose and preserve the installer output. If the management-cluster API is reachable and Cluster API resources were pivoted into it, delete the self-managed cluster with:

nkp delete cluster \
  --cluster-name="${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --kubeconfig="/home/nutanix/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf" \
  --self-managed

The CLI creates a temporary bootstrap cluster, moves the lifecycle resources to it, and deletes the management cluster. Confirm the cluster name and kubeconfig before running this destructive command.

If creation failed before the pivot, the existing konvoy-capi-bootstrapper kind cluster can still own the Cluster API resources. Preserve it and inspect kubectl get clusters,machines -A with its kubeconfig before cleanup. Do not start by deleting VMs in Prism Central or removing finalizers; doing so can leave managed resources behind.

docs.title: Which namespace contains the management cluster?
docs.text:
Discover it instead of assuming:

kubectl get clusters -A

Management clusters upgraded from NKP 2.17 commonly retain the default namespace. Newer deployments can use kommander. Use the namespace reported by the resource in CLI commands.

docs.title: Can I skip an intermediate NKP release during an upgrade?
docs.text:
NKP 2.18 can upgrade directly to NKP 2.19.0.

Do not generalize this to other versions. Direct upgrade from 2.17.x to 2.19.0 is not supported because it skips the 2.18 minor release. Always confirm the exact source and target versions in the release-specific upgrade path.

Upgrade the management plane and verify it before upgrading managed workload clusters.

docs.title: Which NKP CLI version should I use?
docs.text:
Use the CLI required by the operation and target release. During an upgrade, retain the previous CLI until every dependent environment has reached the target version.

Always verify before running a lifecycle command:

nkp version

docs.title: What should I collect before asking for support?
docs.text:
Record:

  • NKP CLI and cluster versions;
  • affected cluster name and namespace;
  • when the issue started and the last known change;
  • relevant Cluster API conditions and events;
  • whether the environment is connected, restricted, or air-gapped;
  • a support bundle from the affected management or workload cluster.

Follow the Support bundle guide.

docs.title: Create a support bundle
docs.text:
The NKP CLI generates diagnostic archives with nkp diagnose. A bundle can include Kubernetes resources, pod logs, cluster information, and node-level diagnostics.

Commands on this page were checked with the NKP 2.17.1 CLI. Run nkp diagnose --help with the CLI matching your environment because flags and collectors can change between releases.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the NKP CLI matching the environment;
  • a working kubeconfig for the affected cluster;
  • sufficient permissions to read cluster resources, logs, and secrets and to run the diagnostic node collector;
  • enough local disk space for the resulting archive;
  • access to the diagnostic collector images.

The default node collector runs a privileged pod with host access. Follow your organization's change and security process before collecting diagnostics.

Support bundles contain sensitive data

A bundle can contain logs, Kubernetes resources, Secrets, certificates, endpoint names, IP addresses, and infrastructure details. Store it securely, inspect it before sharing, and upload it only through an approved support channel.

docs.title: Check the CLI and access
docs.text:
nkp version
nkp diagnose --help
kubectl --kubeconfig <path-to-kubeconfig> cluster-info
kubectl --kubeconfig <path-to-kubeconfig> get nodes

Use an administrative identity or an approved diagnostic role. By default, the CLI can still produce a partial bundle when some collectors lack permission. Record permission failures because the missing data can affect troubleshooting.

docs.title: Collect from the management cluster
docs.text:
Create a dedicated local directory:

mkdir -p "$HOME/nkp-support"
cd "$HOME/nkp-support"

Collect the last 24 hours:

export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf"

nkp diagnose \
  --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  --since 24h \
  --bundle-name-prefix "management-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-"

The CLI writes the compressed support bundle to the current directory and reports its filename.

Use --since-time instead of --since when the incident has a known UTC start time:

nkp diagnose \
  --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" \
  --since-time "2026-07-14T07:00:00Z" \
  --bundle-name-prefix "management-incident-"

docs.title: Collect from a workload cluster
docs.text:
Use the affected workload cluster's kubeconfig:

export WORKLOAD_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-dev-cluster.conf"

nkp diagnose \
  --kubeconfig "${WORKLOAD_KUBECONFIG}" \
  --since 24h \
  --bundle-name-prefix "nkp-dev-cluster-"

For lifecycle or fleet-management incidents, collect a management-cluster bundle as well as a bundle from the affected workload cluster.

docs.title: Include the temporary bootstrap cluster
docs.text:
During management-cluster provisioning, collect data from both the target and temporary kind cluster when they are reachable:

kind get kubeconfig --name konvoy-capi-bootstrapper > bootstrap-cluster.conf

nkp diagnose \
  --kubeconfig "$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf" \
  --bootstrap-kubeconfig bootstrap-cluster.conf \
  --since 4h \
  --bundle-name-prefix "management-bootstrap-"

If the target management-cluster API is not yet available, preserve the bootstrap kubeconfig and collect the Cluster API resources, controller logs, and events directly before deleting the kind cluster.

docs.title: Inspect the configured collectors
docs.text:
Display the default support-bundle specification:

nkp diagnose default-config

The default specification shows the exact images and collectors used by that CLI version. It commonly includes cluster resources, all namespace logs, Secrets, and privileged node diagnostics.

This command is especially useful in restricted environments: mirror every referenced collector and pause image before running nkp diagnose.

docs.title: Optional SSH node diagnostics
docs.text:
The CLI can collect directly from nodes over SSH:

nkp diagnose ssh path/to/inventory-file.yaml \
  --bundle-name-prefix "node-diagnostics-" \
  --timeout 10m

Use this mode when Kubernetes-based node collectors cannot run or when Nutanix support requests it. Protect the inventory file because it can contain node addresses and access information. Check the inventory format required by the installed release before use:

nkp diagnose ssh --help

docs.title: Review and transfer the archive
docs.text:
Identify and inspect the generated archive:

ls -lh *.tar.gz
tar -tzf <support-bundle>.tar.gz
shasum -a 256 <support-bundle>.tar.gz

Extract it only into a protected directory if content review is required. Do not attach support bundles to public issues, chat rooms, or source repositories.

docs.title: Collector pods cannot pull images
docs.text: Mirror the images shown by nkp diagnose default-config and confirm the cluster's registry configuration. This is common in air-gapped environments.

docs.title: The bundle reports permission errors
docs.text: Use an approved identity with broader diagnostic access, or share the partial bundle together with the permission errors. Do not assume that a generated archive is complete.

docs.title: Collection times out
docs.text: Reduce the log window with --since, check unhealthy nodes and API connectivity, or increase the per-node timeout for nkp diagnose ssh.

docs.title: TLS validation fails
docs.text: Prefer a trusted certificate authority and the correct server name. Options that disable certificate verification are intended only for controlled diagnostics and expose the connection to interception.

docs.title: Upgrade paths
docs.text: Upgrade guides are separated by target version because supported upgrade paths, Kubernetes versions, and image requirements vary between NKP releases.

docs.title: Supported paths
docs.text:
NKP 2.18 can upgrade directly to NKP 2.19.0:

flowchart LR
    a["NKP 2.18"] --> b["NKP 2.19.0"]

Choose the applicable path:

  • Upgrade from NKP 2.18.x to 2.19.0

Do not skip minor releases

Direct upgrade from NKP 2.17.x to 2.19.0 is not supported. Upgrade to NKP 2.18 first, using the 2.18 version of this documentation. Use the version selector in the header to switch versions.

docs.title: Before any upgrade
docs.text:
• Confirm that the source and target versions form a supported upgrade path.
  • Read the release notes and compatibility information.
  • Back up important cluster and application data.
  • Check management and workload cluster health.
  • Make the target node image available in Prism Central.
  • Review the complete version-specific procedure before running commands.

docs.title: Choose a workflow
docs.text:
Determine whether GitOps or the NKP CLI owns the cluster definition. Do not use an imperative CLI upgrade for a cluster whose desired state is reconciled from Git.

Treat an upgrade as a rolling infrastructure change

Cluster API can replace nodes during a Kubernetes upgrade. Check application replicas, disruption budgets, storage attachment behavior, and spare capacity before starting.

Select the applicable upgrade guide from the navigation.

Field note: finish each stage across the fleet

Upgrade and verify the management cluster, platform applications, and managed workload clusters in controlled batches. Running a fleet across several upgrade stages makes CLI compatibility and troubleshooting harder.

docs.title: Upgrade NKP from 2.18.x to 2.19.0
docs.text:
This procedure upgrades the NKP platform and then moves the management cluster and workload clusters to Kubernetes 1.36.2 with the Rocky Linux 9.8 node image.

Upgrade through 2.18 first

NKP 2.17.x clusters cannot upgrade directly to 2.19.0. Follow the 2.18 version of this documentation, then return here. Use the version selector in the header to switch versions.

docs.title: Infrastructure versions
docs.text:
NKP 2.19.0 supports Prism Central pc.7.5 and pc.7.6, and AOS 7.5 and 7.6. Upgrade Prism Central and AOS before NKP if you are on an older version.

Ubuntu vGPU

The NKP 2.19 support matrix no longer lists vGPU for Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, and NKP 2.18 did. If you use vGPU on Ubuntu, confirm support before you upgrade.

docs.title: Prism Central Projects 2.0
docs.text:
A Nutanix cluster must use one Prism Central project for all its resources, including the control plane, every worker pool, and volume groups. If a 2.18 cluster spans projects, for example a control plane in the default project and GPU pools in a user-defined project, move all nodes into one project before the upgrade.

NKP 2.19 introduces the unified --pc-project=<project-name> flag. Omit it for the default project, which resolves to _internal. The older --control-plane-pc-project and --worker-pc-project flags are deprecated, so update any scripts that use them. A user-defined project requires Prism Central, Prism Element, and AOS 7.6 or later.

Plan this early

Changing a cluster's project after creation is not supported. A cluster that must move into a user-defined project might need Nutanix Support to migrate existing volume groups. Do not leave this for the maintenance window.

docs.title: Registry credentials
docs.text: Management clusters without a Nutanix Docker Hub registry token must provide one during the upgrade. A regular Docker Hub account does not grant access to the Nutanix repository. nkp upgrade kommander checks for the token at the start and stops if it is missing.

docs.title: Catalogs and automation
docs.text:
• Migrate remaining AppDeployment resources from GitRepository catalogs to OCIRepository catalogs. GitRepository catalogs are no longer supported.
  • Remove --kommander-applications-repository from scripts and pipelines. It is no longer supported by nkp install kommander and nkp upgrade kommander.
  • nkp upgrade workspace is deprecated. Use the cluster and platform application upgrade steps below.

docs.title: Known limitation: single-instance Nutanix Enterprise AI
docs.text: A single-instance Nutanix Enterprise AI deployment can block worker nodes from draining during a cluster upgrade. Check the 2.19 release notes for the documented adjustment before you start.

docs.title: Fleet health
docs.text:
Every management and workload cluster must be on NKP 2.18 and healthy. Verify backups, spare capacity for rolling replacement, disruption budgets, and Cluster API health. All platform applications on a workload cluster must be healthy before you upgrade it.

export MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG="$HOME/nkp-mgmt-cluster.conf"
export KUBECONFIG="${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}"

kubectl get nodes
kubectl get clusters -A
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl get helmreleases -A --no-headers | grep -v "True" || echo "ALL APPS READY"

docs.title: Required upgrade sequence
docs.text:
1. Upgrade Kommander on the management cluster.
  2. Upgrade the management cluster Kubernetes version and node image.
  3. Upgrade each workload cluster, from the UI or with the CLI.

Never upgrade a workload cluster before its management cluster.

docs.title: Prepare the artifacts
docs.text:
Install the NKP 2.19 CLI. Keep the 2.18 binary while the fleet contains both releases.

tar -xvzf nkp-bundle_v2.19.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
sudo install -m 0755 ./nkp-v2.19.0/cli/nkp /usr/local/bin/nkp
nkp version

Upload the NKP 2.19 node image to Prism Central. Download it from the Nutanix Support Portal under NKP Operating System Images, verify the published checksum, and do not rename it. For air-gapped environments or custom images, see Node images.

export TARGET_VM_IMAGE=nkp-rocky-9.8-release-cis-1.36.2.qcow2

The filename is an example. Use the exact name in Prism Central.

docs.title: Upgrade Kommander
docs.text:
nkp upgrade kommander --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}"
kubectl get helmreleases -A --no-headers | grep -v "True" || echo "ALL APPS READY"

The command runs checks first, then upgrades the management plane and platform applications. It can show no output for several minutes. To follow progress, watch the HelmReleases from a second terminal.

Field note: expect to log in again

After the Kommander upgrade the authentication token changes and the UI returns to the login screen. Token-based kubeconfigs stop working, but a certificate-based administrator kubeconfig keeps working.

docs.title: Upgrade the clusters
docs.text:
After nkp upgrade kommander, you can upgrade each cluster from the NKP UI. No further CLI commands are needed. The CLI still works and follows the same structure as the 2.18 upgrade. Choose one method per cluster and do not mix them.

Upgrade the management cluster first, then the workload clusters. For ClusterClass clusters, the workflow upgrades platform applications first, then Kubernetes and the cluster infrastructure.

docs.title: Option 1: NKP UI
docs.text:
1. Open Administration → Upgrades.
  2. Choose the cluster and select NKP 2.19.0.
  3. Select the new node image for the control plane and each node pool.
  4. Start the upgrade and follow it in the upgrade tracker.

The pre-checks always run from the UI. Upgrade clusters in controlled batches and verify each one before starting the next.

docs.title: Option 2: NKP CLI
docs.text:
Discover the cluster name and namespace instead of guessing them:

kubectl get clusters -A

export CLUSTER_NAME=nkp-mgmt-cluster
export CLUSTER_NAMESPACE=kommander

nkp upgrade cluster nutanix \
  --cluster-name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${CLUSTER_NAMESPACE}" \
  --vm-image "${TARGET_VM_IMAGE}" \
  --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}"

Run it for the management cluster first and wait until it is healthy. Then repeat it for each workload cluster, using that cluster's name and namespace, which is usually its workspace.

For clusters that are not ClusterClass-based, upgrade platform applications with nkp upgrade platform-apps, then follow the cluster-specific procedure.

When Flux owns the cluster definition, update the declared Kubernetes version and node image in Git instead. Do not combine imperative and GitOps ownership.

Cluster API replaces the nodes one by one. Wait until all nodes are Ready on Kubernetes 1.36.2 and all applications are healthy before moving on.

Field note: a yellow warning is not a failure

Early in the Kubernetes step, the upgrade tracker can warn that a BeforeClusterUpgrade hook timed out. Cluster API retries on its own. Wait a few minutes before changing anything.

docs.title: Replace Kubernetes Dashboard
docs.text: NKP 2.19 replaces Kubernetes Dashboard with Headlamp. An upgraded cluster keeps the existing Dashboard running and leaves Headlamp disabled until you enable it. Nutanix recommends migrating to Headlamp as soon as possible.

docs.title: Monitor and verify
docs.text:
kubectl get clusters,machines -A
kubectl get kubeadmcontrolplanes,machinedeployments -A

kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" get nodes
kubectl --kubeconfig "${MANAGEMENT_KUBECONFIG}" get pods -A
kubectl --kubeconfig "$HOME/${WORKLOAD_CLUSTER_NAME}.conf" get nodes
kubectl --kubeconfig "$HOME/${WORKLOAD_CLUSTER_NAME}.conf" get pods -A

Confirm Cluster API readiness, application health, storage, external endpoints, monitoring, and backups. Remove the old Rocky Linux 9.7 node image from Prism Central only after no virtual machine uses it.
